catalog_quote: Таким образом, облеченное важной смысловой функцией абазинское ударение не имеет определенного места в слове и встречаются слова всех возможных типов ударения (на первом, втором, третьем и т. д. слоге многочисленного слова). Ударение словесное. Необходимо различать по крайней мере два вида ударения: ударение отдельного слова, ударение словесное и ударение словосочетания — ударение синтаксическое. ... Ударение неподвижное. По ударению слова абазинского языка разделяются на два основных типа: слова с неподвижным ударением и слова с подвижным ударением; при этом передвижение ударения происходит при присоединении к имеющей реальное значение основе слова известных, нормально лишенных своего ударения служебных морфем (сюда относятся падежные окончания, окончания времени, наклонения и т. п.). К первой категории относятся: 1) те слова, основа которых состоит из одного закрытого слога ... 2) слова с двусложной или многосложной основой, с ударением не на последнем слоге

new_statements.translation: Thus Abaza stress, which carries an important meaning-distinguishing function, has no fixed place in the word, and words of all possible stress types occur (on the first, second, third etc. syllable of a polysyllabic [lit. 'numerous'] word). [...] Fixed stress. By their stress the words of Abaza divide into two basic types: words with fixed stress and words with mobile stress; the shift of stress takes place when certain auxiliary morphemes, normally lacking a stress of their own (case endings, tense and mood endings, etc.), are attached to the lexical stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Free (non-fixed), strongly distinctive dynamic word stress: any syllable of the word may carry it and many word pairs differ only in stress placement (а́ла 'eye' vs ала́ 'dog', а́сра 'beat' vs асра́ 'weave'). Placement is lexically and morphologically determined: closed-monosyllabic stems and polysyllabic stems with non-final stress keep stress fixed under affixation; open-monosyllabic (CV) stems have mobile stress that shifts forward onto stress-accepting suffixes or back onto prefixes (article a-), while a class of suffixes (-la instrumental, -ta, -da, most derivational formants) never accepts stress. In later comparative terms (Dybo 1977/2000/2007, Spruit 1986, Moroz & Kuznetsova 2022) morphemes/syllables are dominant or recessive and stress falls on the first dominant element that is followed by a recessive one or by the word end (all-recessive words: Dybo says final, Moroz & Kuznetsova say initial).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Genko p. 66: long predicative (verbal) complexes may carry two stresses, 'the second weakened' (уыгIасзынхатIд 'you remained for me'); Lomtatidze 2006 p. 112: complex stems and compounds have one main stress, 'sometimes a co-stress of lesser force is possible'. No rhythmic secondary stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Genko p. 65-66: isolated unmotivated deviations (лы́мхIа 'ear' but лымхIа́ла; та́ба 'pan' but таба́ла); compound and predicative-complex stress 'not reducible to simple formulas'; interrogative -ma takes stress in the Karapago (Kuvinsk) subdialect unlike Tapanta proper and Abkhaz; many polysyllabic loans (революца, бригада) have fixed stress. Phonetically Genko notes Abaza stress involves no noticeable pitch rise or lengthening and is harder to hear than Russian or Abkhaz stress (p. 63); Dybo, Nikolaev & Starostin 1978 claim a high/low tone distinction on the stressed syllable in Tapanta.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('udarenie slovesnoe') on citation and inflected forms; Genko separately treats phrase-level 'syntactic' stress (one word of a close-knit phrase made more prominent, others keeping weakened stress) and 'logical' (emphatic) stress, and hiatus resolution merging phrase-mates into one phonetic word.
new_statements.identity_note: Genko 1955 explicitly describes the Tapanta dialect (narechie tapanta; Glottolog tapa1257), the basis of literary Abaza; Klychev & Chkadua 1999 and Lomtatidze 2006 describe literary Abaza (Tapanta-based, with Ashkharywa/ashk1234 notes). Moroz & Kuznetsova's 2022 draft covers Tapanta as spoken in Inzhich-Chukun and Krasnyj Vostok (Gumlokt). Lomtatidze 2006 is the Russian original of the text published in English as Lomtatidze & Klychev 1989 'Abaza' (Hewitt ed.), i.e. the source the earlier scan named as unreachable.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Abaza is mobile, distinctive and is determined by inherent properties of morphemes, cf. minimal pairs ʕá-j-ra CISL-come-MSD ‘to come’ vs. ʕa-j-rá CISL-grow-MSD ‘to grow’ (Moroz 2017). [...] Each morpheme (more precisely, CV(C) formative) is assigned to one of the following accentual classes: Dominant (D), Recessive (R), Fixed stress (F). The accentual class is a lexical property of each morpheme not correlated with any synchronic phonological or grammatical properties. [...] (1) a. If the word contains F formatives, the stress falls on the first F formative, otherwise b. If the word contains D formatives, the stress falls on the first D formative not followed by another D formative, otherwise c. If the word contains only R formatives, the stress falls on the first syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Genko 1955 statement (stress distinctive, no fixed place in the word, words of every stress position occur) and with the catalog's empty-rule Abaza record; adds the explicit morpheme-class (D/R/F) accentuation algorithm after Dybo/Spruit/Moroz, the default-initial clause for all-Recessive words, the statement that there is no word-level tone, and the nominal-complex stress-domain note. Terminology differs from Genko's 'Ударение неподвижное': Arkadiev calls stress 'mobile' because its position shifts across inflected forms of one lexeme (sə́-la 'my eye' vs la-kwá 'eyes'), which Genko treats under exceptions; this is a difference of framing, not of placement type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive and not fixed to any position; every CV(C) formative carries a lexically specified accent class (Dominant, Recessive, or Fixed), and the stressed syllable is computed from the string of classes: the first Fixed formative wins; failing that, the first Dominant formative not followed by another Dominant; a word made only of Recessive formatives is stressed on its first syllable. The system is said to work like Abkhaz (Spruit 1985; Dybo 1977, 2000); the negation prefix m(ə)- copies the accent class of the following morpheme. Same section adds: Genko (1955: 63) calls the stress dynamic but this is not instrumentally verified; stress is unmarked in orthography and only Tugov (1967) marks it (headwords only); 'Abaza has no phonological word-level tone. Sentence intonation has not been investigated.' Unstressed /ə/ deletes (2.5, rule b).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. On domain: section 4.1 (p. 63) says monosyllabic numerals and adjectives 'clearly form a single stress domain with the head noun' in the nominal complex (truba–ʕʷáž’-kʷa-ḳ 'yellow pipes'), and reports Tabulova (1976: 68) as saying stress in the nominal complex falls on the last lexical unit, 'however, this remains to be tested empirically'.
new_statements.exceptions: Negation marker m(ə)- assimilates its accentual class to the following morpheme (ex. 7); the ethnonym abáza marks plural by shifting stress to the first syllable (ábaza, section 3.2.3); short (unstressed) vs full (stressed) personal pronouns sa(rá) etc. (3.4.1); some CCə morphemes metathesize to CəC when unstressed (2.5, rule c).
new_statements.identity_note: Arkadiev's sketch is explicitly based on the Tapanta dialect (the written standard and the speech of Inžič-Čukun, fieldwork 2017-2019), the same dialect as Genko 1955 ('narečie tapanta'); the stress examples are credited to Moroz (2017, 2018) fieldwork in Inžič-Čukun. Ashkharywa Abaza is not covered.

new_statements.quote: According to Genko (1955: 63), stress in Abaza is dynamic; this, however, has not been independently proven by instrumental analysis. Despite its unpredictability and its role in grammar, Abaza stress is not marked in the orthography, including most of the examples in existing grammars; moreover, of the existing dictionaries only Tugov (1967) marks stress, but just in the headwords. Abaza has no phonological word-level tone. Sentence intonation has not been investigated.

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Ударение в абазинском динамическое, интенсивное, не фиксированное: а́лагара ‘начать’, гы́лра ‘вставать’, аща́ ‘брат’, ауа́са ‘так’, ажвра́ ‘варить’, напIы́ ‘рука’. Слова или те или иные формы одного и того же слова весьма часто разнятся между собой только по месту ударения, например: а́ла ‘глаз’ — ала́ ‘собака’; а́чва ‘сон’ — ачва́ ‘кожа’; пхядзара́ ‘считать’ — пхядза́ра ‘счет’, ‘число’ и т. д. Такое противопоставление слов или форм по месту ударения — обычно результат различного морфологического или лексического состава указанных основ. Ударение в основном подвижное: в одной и той же именной и глагольной основе оно может передвигаться с одного слога на другой в зависимости от формообразования и формоизменения. Более устойчиво в этом отношении ударение, падающее на слог, который находится в середине основы.
sources.note: Stress is dynamic, intensive, not fixed; minimal pairs by stress place (а́ла ‘eye’ / ала́ ‘dog’; а́чва ‘sleep’ / ачва́ ‘skin’; пхядзара́ ‘to count’ / пхядза́ра ‘count, number’), which she attributes to differing morphological/lexical make-up of the stems; stress is mostly mobile within one nominal or verbal stem under inflection and derivation, and more stable when it falls on a stem-medial syllable. Weight/quantity: not mentioned. Secondary stress: not mentioned (catalog sec_status ‘stated: exists, placement not given’ rests on Genko 1955, not on this chapter). Tone: not mentioned anywhere in

sources.note: 'Stress in Abaza is distinctive (saˈɾa «I» vs. ˈsaɾa «lamb»). Each Abaza morpheme.. can be represented by combination of open syllables with vowel a or ə.. each syllable assigned to one of the accentual classes: dominant or recessive. The main stress rule is formulated in (Spruit 1986: 37-40): stress falls on the first D element followed by R or word boundary, otherwise stress is on the first syllable.' Based on 50 minimal pairs recorded from 13 speakers; unfinished draft.

sources.note: Comparative: Abkhaz, Tapanta (Abaza) and Ubykh preserve the West Caucasian paradigmatic accent system; morphemes are dominant or recessive (-) and 'ударение всегда ставится в конце первой последовательности морфем высшей валентности' (stress at the end of the first sequence of highest-valency morphemes; all-recessive words get final stress). Notes Starostin seemed to detect weak tones in Tapanta; complains Abaza dictionaries omit stress marks although 'роль ударения в абазинском языке неизмеримо выше, чем в русском'.
sources.venue: Lingvisticheskaja komparativistika v kul'turnom i istoricheskom aspektakh

tone.quote: Dybo et al. (1978: 17) suggest that two tones, high and low, are distinguished on the stressed syllable in Tapanta Abaza. According to their analysis, high tone is found on so-called dominant morphemes, and low tone corresponds to recessive morphemes (see Borise-stress (this volume), section 6.1.2 for morpheme classification in Abkhaz-Abaza). However, the original analysis was not based on instrumental findings, and instrumental data collected during recent fieldwork (2017-2018) did not lend support to the tonal analysis (Peter Arkadiev, p.c.).
tone.locator: preprint (page 4), section 2.2 'Tonal contrasts on stressed syllables'; = p. 761 of the published chapter (so cited by Andersson 2024: 'Borise 2021a: 761')
tone.summary: No tonal analysis reported for Abkhaz; sister Tapanta Abaza's claimed H/L an earlier reading tone unsupported instrumentally.
